extracted.intended_audience: maritime historians, shipping researchers, and enthusiasts of 19th‑century sailing ships
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and evaluating measures used to judge the performance, seaworthiness, passenger accommodation, and operational readiness of 19th‑century clippers and merchant sailing ships (passages to Australia and related trades).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage time (Days Out / under 80 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables listing voyages labelled “PASSAGES UNDER 80 DAYS” and a final column “Days Out” that record the total number of days for an outward passage (used to identify fast passages and records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author compiles every outward passage under 80 days where possible; slips may occur and blank entries are left where proof was lacking. These totals are used to identify notable fast passages and compare ships across years (e.g., best passages to Sydney or Melbourne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passage milestones (departure, equator, meridian, cape, arrival)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voyage tables record intermediate milestones such as Departure, Crossed Equator (with longitude), Crossed Cape Meridian, Passed S.W. Cape / Otway / Hobson’s Bay, and Arrival (port).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milestones are used to reconstruct route and timing; the author notes that where documentary proof is lacking a date is left blank. These checkpoints allow calculation of segment times (e.g., days to the Otway) and comparison of routes/strategies between voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short-interval run distances (best day’s work, best week’s work, average miles/day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative reports include short-interval performance metrics: best day’s run (e.g., 336 miles), best week’s work (e.g., 2055 miles), and average miles per day over multi‑day runs (e.g., averaged 276 miles/day for 19 days).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such 24‑hour and weekly figures are used to characterize a ship’s peak and sustained performance, and to explain why a ship did or did not break records (e.g., calms that reduced otherwise record-breaking runs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship speed and ability to maintain knots
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of typical or sustained speed in knots for a ship: e.g., “with a moderately fresh breeze will maintain a speed of 10 or 11 knots.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to summarize operational performance in representative conditions rather than isolated fast runs; complements day/mile metrics to assess overall capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design and rigging for speed (spar plan, sail area, mast placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design and rigging details that affect speed and handling: spar plans and measurements, mast placement (e.g., mainmast stepped amidships), short topgallant masts with fidded royal and skysail masts, overmasting (double topgallant yards and skysails), and overall sail plan (extent of canvas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical dimensions and rigging choices are cited to explain why a vessel is an ‘out and out racer’ or conversely overmasted and later cut down; these are direct determinants of speed and handling in different wind conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger accommodation quality and amenities
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of passenger comforts and layout: spacious saloon (e.g., 80 feet long, berthing for 60), cabins 10 ft square with lavatory and chest of drawers, large windows with controllable ventilation, bathroom with hot and cold baths, saloon skylights, piano, tables removable to clear for dancing, and a smoking‑room for gentlemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to judge the degree of passenger luxury and practicality. The author contrasts ‘absolutely luxurious’ fittings with ‘solid and material comfort’, noting owners who fit out cabins like hotel bedrooms; these details indicate how ships were marketed and fitted for passenger trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Galley and fresh water supply capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational provisioning capacities such as galley cooking capacity and water distillation: e.g., galley capable of cooking for 500 people and a steam condenser able to distil 500 gallons daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistical capabilities (food production and potable water supply) are key criteria for long voyages, suitability for passenger trade, and survival of live freight; cited as concrete engineering/operational measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisioning and lifeboat preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: System for provisioning lifeboats: ability for apprentices to provision boats for all hands for 14 days in two minutes; falls always kept rove; each lifeboat stocked with two 15‑gallon breakers kept full of fresh water, tins of biscuits and meat, and a third box with medical comforts, clothing, tobacco, hatchet, knives, compass, plus lifeboat sails and necessary gear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a best-practice safety system; Captain Horne suggests making such plans compulsory. This is a concrete safety/readiness rubric: how quickly and effectively lifeboats can be provisioned and equipped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seamanship and captain’s decisions in heavy weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of captainly decisions affecting survival and performance: standing off to the east side of a bay to avoid a cyclone; foresight in shortening sail; rigging jury masts after dismasting; deliberate jettisoning of cargo to save the ship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These narrative examples are used as evaluative criteria for good command and skill: foresight, risk avoidance, and damage‑control measures determine whether a ship survives severe weather and the extent of subsequent repairs/costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seaworthiness and behavior under load (‘no vices’)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgements of a ship’s inherent handling characteristics: e.g., “a ship that has got no vices and when properly loaded is as gentle as a lamb,” and whether a ship is a ‘good light weather ship’ or ‘not a ship of excessive speed’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such qualitative assessments (lack of vices, gentleness, behavior when properly loaded) are criteria for crew preference, predictability, and safety; they often trade off with outright speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live freight suitability and animal welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that a ship can carry live animals safely and in good condition: accounts of voyages that landed horses and camels alive and in prime condition, contrasted with other vessels that lost most animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful carriage of live freight is cited as a criterion of crew skill, provisioning, and ship suitability (stowage, ventilation, and stability) for special cargoes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Race performance and competitiveness (racing for wool sales)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative and race metrics: instances of ships racing to catch wool sales, ships ‘in company’ and being outpaced or romping away, and direct comparisons between named vessels (e.g., Cutty Sark vs Thomas Stephens; Thessalus vs Cimba).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess relative performance in real operational competition rather than isolated runs; context (cargo, loading, calms) is noted as explanatory when races do not produce expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance, refit history and classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of repair/refit after damage, time to re‑rig and cost (e.g., rerigged in 10 days; refit cost £9071), being classed 100 A1, and being raised and restored as ‘as good as the day she was launched’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refit capability, cost, classification grades and swiftness of repairs are used to judge longevity, economic viability, and continued seaworthiness of a vessel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance, valuation and economic outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Financial indicators tied to ship condition/trouble: amounts insured (e.g., insurances amounting to £30,000), being described as ‘uninsurable at 90 guineas’, sale prices (e.g., sold for scrap iron price of £1800), and sale/renaming after perceived damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insurance status and sale value are treated as objective measures of perceived risk, condition and commercial viability; being uninsurable or having low resale value signals serious problems or age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic appearance and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments of a ship’s visual and reputational attributes: ‘majestic appearance’, ‘magnificent clipper’, painted schemes (e.g., Aberdeen green with white masts), and the striking look of fully squared yards in port.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While subjective, appearance is presented as part of a ship’s reputation and commercial appeal; it factors into owners’ pride and may influence passenger preference and perceived quality.
